task.title: One page to switch between local project boards
task.description:
Each workbook serve is scoped to a single repository: openServiceParts (internal/cli/run.go:1066) opens the repo at cwd, and the web handler is built entirely from closures over that one repo's service — internal/webui has no notion of a project beyond the one it was started in. With multiple local repositories using Workbook, that means one browser tab per board on a different port each, and no way to see or switch between projects from a single place. The goal is the Linear model: one page with the projects in a sidebar, click to switch boards.

The architecture is an open question and answering it is part of this story. Candidate directions, roughly in order of increasing invasiveness:

1. A hub page over per-repo servers. Each repository keeps its own serve process (the automatic port selection story makes this workable); running servers register themselves in a well-known user-level location (e.g. a registry file with repo path, project name, address, pid), and a small hub page discovers them and presents the sidebar, navigating or embedding across servers. Minimal change to the existing single-repo server.

2. A multi-repo server. One serve process opens several repositories — each with its own service, publisher, and sync watcher — and the board API and UI become project-aware (project list endpoint, project segment in API routes, sidebar in the board itself). Closest to the Linear experience but touches the whole handler surface and per-repo lifecycle management.

The design decision (and its rationale — what was rejected and why) should be recorded before implementation, following the repository's planning conventions. Whichever direction wins, the per-repo git-based storage model is not in question; this is about presentation and process topology, not moving task data out of repositories.

Acceptance criteria:
- There is one URL to open that shows all locally known Workbook projects and lets the user switch between their boards without hand-managing ports or tabs.
- Projects are listed by a human-readable name, not by filesystem path alone.
- Opening a project's board from the switcher yields the full existing board experience: task lanes, detail view, mutations, and optimistic rendering all work unchanged.
- A project whose server or repository is unavailable is shown as such rather than breaking the switcher page.
- Adding a new local Workbook repository makes it appear in the switcher through a documented mechanism (automatic registration or an explicit command), without editing internal files by hand.
- The chosen architecture is written down with the trade-offs considered before the implementation lands.
